rv.q: This stage adaptation is a worthy addition to the canon.

Carré’s enthralling plot is deftly adapted for the stage by Eldridge, brought to life under Herrin’s meticulous direction, creating a captivating examination of betrayal, love and the high stakes nature of Alec’s last assignment.
Fans of spy shenanigans and Cold War political machinations will be instantly swept up in this lean, pacy adaptation.
Mostly, Eldridge and co make the case for the 62-year-old novel’s enduring appeal, with Keenan’s study in disillusionment crossed with dogged determination really clinching the deal.
Le Carre’s plot still snakes craftily to its wintry conclusion: that intelligence services are driven by a single moral imperative - results.
It is to Le Carré’s credit that this fundamentally nihilistic thesis makes for cracking reading – and, in the end, a suitably thrilling stage play.
But those unfamiliar with the source material may feel somewhat left out in the cold.
This has still been a tale exhilaratingly told, and if it fails it fails for being too inventive in developing Smiley’s character, rather than not inventive enough.

Likewise, the final episode at the Berlin Wall gets, in Jeremy Herrin’s fast-paced production, a neat coup de theatre that is very enjoyable. But for me the main problem with this play is the first half.
Yet neither survive intact in Eldridge’s new play, however niftily he condenses the book’s labyrinthian twists and turns.
Jeremy Herrin's production of the first John Le Carré novel to be adapted to the stage is, sadly, a lukewarm dramatisation of a Cold War classic.
This is still an enjoyable couple of hours in the theatre

cn.t: Le Carré's first stage adaptation receives mixed reviews. Critics praise the stylish production and strong performances, but many find the brisk pacing sacrifices atmosphere and complexity, making the intricate plot hard to follow.
